A predilection is a strong, personal preference for something — a deep, settled liking that feels natural to who you are. It is not a passing interest or a casual choice. It is a preference that feels like it is part of you, something you are consistently drawn toward.

Think of it this way: if you simply choose coffee over tea today, that is a preference. But if you always gravitate toward coffee, love everything about it, and feel an almost instinctive pull toward it — that is closer to a predilection.

A predilection has three key qualities baked into it:

1. It is strong. It goes beyond a mild "I kind of like this." It is a genuine, noticeable inclination.

2. It is settled. It is not new or temporary. A predilection is a preference that has taken root in you. It is characteristic of you.

3. It is personal. It reflects your particular taste, personality, or nature — not just a random choice. It says something about who you are.

• "She has a predilection for dark chocolate."

This means she strongly prefers dark chocolate, consistently, in a way that is just her thing.

  • "The architect showed a predilection for minimalist design."

His preference for clean, simple design was deep and consistent — it showed up in all his work.

  • "He has a predilection for staying up late."

He has a strong, natural inclination to be a night owl. It is not a one-time thing — it is simply how he tends to operate.

  • "The writer had a predilection for melancholy themes."

She was naturally and consistently drawn to sad, heavy themes in her stories.

You will almost always see this word followed by "for":

a predilection for something

That is its most natural structure. You do not say "a predilection to" or "a predilection of." It is always for.

Think of it on a scale from mild to extreme:

Mild interest → Preference → Predilection → Obsession

A predilection sits comfortably in the upper-middle of that range. It is meaningfully stronger than a simple preference, but it does not suggest you cannot live without something. It just means you are clearly, consistently, and naturally drawn to it.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are close cousins of "predilection," but each has a slightly different flavor:

  • Preference — the most neutral and everyday word. It just means you like one thing more than another. A predilection is a stronger, more established preference.
  • Fondness — this carries warmth and affection (you feel fond of something, like a child feeling fond of a toy). A predilection is more about being drawn toward something than feeling warm toward it.
  • Tendency — this is about behavior (a tendency to do something). A predilection is about liking, not just a behavioral pattern.
  • Penchant — this is the closest synonym. A penchant for something means almost exactly what a predilection does — a strong, natural inclination. They are nearly interchangeable, though "predilection" sounds slightly more formal and deliberate.
  • Partiality — this also means a preference or bias toward something, but it often hints at unfairness (being partial to one person over another, for instance). A predilection is about genuine taste, not bias.

"Predilection" is a formal, sophisticated word. You will see it more often in writing — essays, literary criticism, journalism, formal speech — than in casual everyday conversation. If you say "I have a predilection for jazz," it sounds more refined than "I really love jazz." Both are correct, but the first sounds more polished and deliberate.

This does not mean the word is pretentious — it is perfectly natural in formal contexts. Just know that you would not typically use it in casual small talk.
A Final Way to Remember It

If someone asks you what a predilection is, think of it this way:

A predilection is your deep, personal, and consistent "pull" toward something — a preference that feels like it is part of your nature, not just a random choice of the day.
